newsitem.title: USA: Key fuel pumps from downed TWA jet located.
newsitem.headline: Key fuel pumps from downed TWA jet located.

text.p: Investigators seeking the cause of the crash of TWA Flight 800 have found two critical sections of the jet's fuel probes that could help explain why its centre fuel tank exploded, a spokeswoman said on Thursday.

The probes, used to measure fuel amounts, were located late last week inside the Boeing 747's centre tank where investigators believe the deadly blast was centred, said National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) spokeswoman, Shelly Hazle.

The probes have been one of the most sought-after pieces of the plane's debris that investigators had hoped to find. Recovery teams already had brought up more than 90 percent of the wreckage before this discovery.
One piece of the probes showed signs of what is referred to as petalling, in which the metal is shorn and resembles a fringe, which could be characteristic of a bomb, she said.
However, she cautioned that other pieces of the wreckage also have shown petalling, and investigators determined that aluminum can petal simply by becoming very hot and then hitting water, she said.

Paris-bound Flight 800 exploded and crashed off the coast of Long Island, New York, on July 17, killing all 230 people on board. Investigators maintain there are three possible causes -- a bomb, a missile or a mechanical failure -- but they lack evidence to rule out any of the theories.

The jet's centre tank was practically empty, carrying about 50 to 100 gallons (189 to 378 litres) of fuel, and investigators have been searching for the source of a spark or other electrical source that could have triggered the blast.

The probes carry a low electrical charge that normally would not be enough to blow up the tank, but investigators have speculated that a malfunction, such as an electrical surge, could have been one of a chain of malfunctions that could have combined to cause the crash.
The sections of the probes discovered by divers on the ocean floor have been taken to a laboratory in Washington for testing, Hazle said.
Each section is about one foot (0.3 metre) long, she said, while intact probes are about seven feet (2.1 metres) long.

U.S. Navy recovery divers have not been on the ocean floor to bring up debris since last week because of poor weather conditions, officials said. Their high-powered sonar equipment has detected several more possible targets, however, that could be more of the plane's debris.
A memorial service was held on Thursday at a cemetery in Centre Moriches, New York, not far from where the plane crashed, to mark the 100 days since the disaster.
